opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think there's a real tension in how the term gets used in the investment world. When a lot of VCs say "AGI," they often mean something like a really capable product: an AI that can do a broad range of knowledge-work tasks, maybe a very good assistant or a coding agent that replaces a chunk of a software team. Under that framing, AGI is a big business opportunity. It's a larger market, a new platform shift, like mobile or the cloud, but bigger.

What I worry about is that this framing quietly anchors expectations to a "normal technology" picture of impact. You get a story where AGI arrives, productivity goes up, some companies win enormously, some jobs get disrupted, and the economy grows a bit faster, maybe a few extra percentage points a year. That's a dramatic world by historical standards, but it's still recognizably our world.

When I think about systems that can genuinely do everything a human expert can do, including AI research itself, I think the implications are much more radical than that. If you can run millions of copies of a top researcher, faster than humans and without sleep, you could get a feedback loop where AI accelerates AI progress. That could compress what would have been decades of technological change into a few years. That's not "a bigger SaaS market." It's a potential transformation of who or what is making the important decisions in the world.

So I think the casual use of "AGI" as a product milestone can make people underrate both the upside and the risks. If your mental model is "AGI is the next iPhone," you won't plan for scenarios where the technology outstrips our ability to oversee it, or where power concentrates very quickly in whoever controls the most capable systems. I'd like to see people be more precise. Instead of arguing about whether something "is AGI," ask concrete questions: Can it automate most remote work? Can it substantially speed up AI R&D? Those thresholds have very different consequences, and lumping them together under one buzzword hides the part that matters most.

r001.rationale: It contrasts VCs’ product-focused, broad knowledge-work meaning of AGI with systems that can do everything a human expert can, including AI research, and trigger rapid AI progress.

r002.rationale: It says the product framing can anchor people to a normal-technology picture and lead them to underrate AGI’s impact, but does not say that a lack of major societal change would be treated as evidence that AGI has little transformative impact.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of those places where the terminology really matters, because the word "AGI" is doing a lot of quiet work in people's heads. When a VC says they're investing in a company because it's building AGI, I think what they usually have in mind is something like a really, really good product. A very capable chatbot, or an assistant that can do a lot of white-collar tasks, or a model that scores at the top of all the benchmarks. And that's a totally reasonable thing to be excited about from an investment standpoint, because that's a trillion-dollar product category.

But the thing I worry about is that this framing kind of smuggles in the assumption that the endpoint is a product. It's a thing you sell, it has a market, it competes with other products, and you capture value from it in the normal ways. Whereas the definition I tend to care about, and that I think a lot of people in the safety world care about, is more like: systems that can do essentially everything a human can do that's economically relevant, including doing AI research itself. And once you have that, you're not really in a normal product dynamic anymore. You're in a regime where the thing you built can accelerate its own development, where it can potentially replace the people who built it and the people who funded it, and where the question of who controls it becomes a geopolitical question rather than a question about market share.

So I think the VC usage tends to compress the expected impact. It makes AGI sound like the next iPhone or the next cloud computing, where it's a huge deal but the world still basically looks like the world. And I think if you take the stronger definition seriously, the impact is less like a new product category and more like a new species of economic actor showing up. Those imply really different things about what you should be worried about, how fast things could move, and whether the usual logic of "ship it, grow fast, figure out the externalities later" is even remotely appropriate.

I'll say in fairness that the ambiguity isn't entirely the VCs' fault. The labs themselves have used AGI to mean a bunch of different things depending on who they're talking to, and there's a kind of motivated vagueness where you want it to sound transformative enough to justify huge valuations but not so transformative that regulators get nervous. But the net effect is that a lot of the capital flowing into this space is being deployed by people whose mental model is "big product," and I think that leads them to systematically underweight both the upside and the risk relative to what I actually expect.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts VCs’ “big product” conception—such as a capable chatbot or benchmark leader—with a stronger conception involving economically relevant human tasks, AI research, and potentially self-accelerating development.

r002.rationale: It says VC usage makes AGI sound like a major product while the world remains basically the same, but does not explain that people may treat the lack of major societal change after labeling current or near-term systems AGI as evidence of limited transformative impact.

astra-6.text:
I think “AGI” can mean pretty different things to different people, and that makes it easy to agree on the word without agreeing on the implications. A venture capitalist might use it to mean a system that’s very broadly useful—a system that can do a lot of valuable cognitive tasks—and imagine that fitting into a fairly familiar story of startups, growth, and returns.

What I’m interested in is something closer to AI that can automate essentially all the cognitive work humans do, including the work of developing better AI. That possibility pushes you toward a much less familiar picture. You’re potentially changing the rate of technological progress itself, rather than just creating a very large new industry.

So I’d want to ask what capabilities they actually have in mind. Can the system autonomously do research? Can it replace a team, or does it still need substantial human direction? The label alone doesn’t tell you whether someone is anticipating a powerful tool or a fundamental change in how the economy works.

r001.rationale: It contrasts VCs’ broad-but-familiar view of AGI as useful across valuable cognitive tasks with a more expansive definition that automates essentially all human cognitive work, including AI development.

r002.rationale: It says the AGI label alone does not reveal what capabilities someone expects, but does not explain that a lack of major societal change could be taken as evidence that AGI has little transformative impact.

sol-6.1.text:
I think “AGI” can mean quite different things to different people, and that matters a lot when you’re talking about its impact. A venture capitalist might use it to mean a system that’s broadly useful across lots of tasks—a very big commercial opportunity. But that doesn’t necessarily mean a system that could do essentially all of the work that humans do, including scientific research and developing the next generation of AI.

Those would have very different implications. You can imagine something that generates enormous revenues and changes a lot of industries while still leaving the basic pace of technological progress relatively familiar. If you can automate AI research itself, then you potentially have a feedback loop where better AI helps you build still better AI. That could lead to a much more radical change.

So I’d want to ask: what capabilities are you actually imagining? What work can this system do, how reliably, and at what cost? The label alone doesn’t tell you whether someone is expecting a really successful technology company or a fundamental transformation of the economy.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts a VC’s broad commercial-use definition with the stronger ability to do essentially all human work, including AI research, conveying a milder meaning than the traditional transformative conception.

r002.rationale: It says commercially powerful systems could leave technological progress relatively familiar, but does not explain that calling existing or near-term systems AGI could make people interpret the lack of major societal change as evidence that AGI has little transformative impact.
